chapter: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
title: Chicago's Regal Theater and his parents following him to see Ellington
summary: The Regal on Fridays, bands such as Cab Calloway, Millinder and Carter, and his parents going to see what Ellington had that upset him.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: You mentioned hearing Cab Calloway's band on the air when you were at Tennessee State, right?
Kentucky State. Excuse me. Pardon me. Kentucky State.
But who else -- I guess that was when, what -- was that when you first became familiar with Cab's band, was the radio broadcasts, or --
Yes, in person, at the Regal Theater in Chicago. We, all of us, used to go to the Regal on Fridays and catch the openings, and --
How old were you when you started going to the Regal to hear music?
Who else can you remember seeing there? I think you mentioned Duke, right?
Oh Ellington, yes. Lucky Millinder, Benny Carter. Gee whiz. I can't remember all of them, but everybody used to play there, because it was a beautiful theater, you know?
And it was commercially very gratifying to everyone. It was one of those Balaban and Katz. They had a great chain of theaters in Chicago at that point, you know.

And -- oh, it was a cute thing, when my parents used to watch me, when I was supposed to be studying my homework, my lessons, but there was a disc jockey in Chicago called Bob Hawk, and he used to play Ellington all day and all night. And there was another piano player by the name of -- they used to call him Two Ton Baker, and he could play all the Ellington things on piano, you know. And I would go into a haze when I'd hear those things on the air, and so my parents would follow me right straight to the theater. They wanted to see what the heck has this Ellington guy got that's getting our son upset, you know. And in those days Ellington
was young and very sharp, and my mother was a very nice looking woman, and when Duke walked out on stage my mother's eyes popped out.
My father was funny. He said, "Now, Mary, come on, now," you know.
